posts.title: A Corridor in Bloom
posts.excerpt: Spring has arrived along the B Corridor, bringing colour, life, and a reminder of why this landscape matters. Take a look at what's flowering and what's been buzzing.
posts.body:
Spring has arrived along the B Corridor, bringing colour, life, and a welcome reminder of why this landscape matters. After a long, grey winter, the verges, hedgerows and riverbanks are waking up, and so are the creatures that depend on them.

Walk any stretch of the corridor this month and you will notice the change underfoot. What looked like bare ground in February is now a patchwork of green, threaded with the first flowers of the year.

What's flowering

The earliest colour comes from the humble pioneers of the hedge bank, plants we too often mow away before they have a chance to do their work. This spring, look out for lesser celandine, primrose and cowslip, dandelion, and blackthorn frothing white along the older hedgerows.

What's buzzing

Where there are flowers, there is movement. The first queen bumblebees are out, fresh from hibernation and searching for both food and a place to nest. On warmer afternoons you may catch the season's first butterflies tracing the line of the hedge.

A corridor is only as strong as the stepping stones that make it. Every flowering verge is one more place for life to rest, feed and move on.

How you can help

You don't need a large garden, or any garden at all, to be part of this. The simplest thing most of us can do is also one of the most powerful: leave the mower in the shed a little longer.

posts.title: Community Planting Day: A huge success
posts.excerpt: Viewmount Estate residents, supported by B Corridor and Waterford Trees for Life, planted 70 native Irish hedgerow trees. Here's a look at the day and the impact we're making together.
posts.body:
Residents of Viewmount Estate on the Dunmore Road gathered to plant a native hedgerow in their estate. They were greatly supported by B Corridor members and Waterford Trees for Life. 

70 Irish hedgerow trees were planted and pruned to encourage sidegrowth. They were covered with a biomembrane to suppress grass growth and then mulched on top with wood chips. We look forward to seeing this hedgerow go from strength to strength in the coming years. 

Thank you

To everyone who turned up with a spade and a smile: thank you.
posts.author: B Corridor Team

posts.title: Small Creatures, Big Impact
posts.excerpt: From frogs to fungi, the small but mighty play a huge role in a healthy ecosystem. Discover some of the unsung heroes of the B Corridor.
posts.body:
From frogs to fungi, the small but mighty play a huge role in a healthy ecosystem. They rarely make the headlines, but without them the whole corridor would unravel.

Pollinators move life from flower to flower. Decomposers return nutrients to the soil. Amphibians keep insect numbers in check. Each one is a thread in the web.

The unsung heroes

Next time you walk the corridor, look closely at the edges, the damp corners, the long grass. That's where the real work is happening.

posts.title: What Does Biodiversity Mean to You?
posts.excerpt: The National Biodiversity Data Centre asked people across Ireland a deceptively simple question. From scientists to neighbours, everyone had an answer — here is what we heard.
posts.body:
Ask ten people what biodiversity means and you will get ten different answers. For some it is birdsong on the morning walk; for others it is a half-remembered word from a science class. The National Biodiversity Data Centre put that very question to people across Ireland — and the answers, in the short film below, are well worth a watch.

A word that means many things

At its simplest, biodiversity is the variety of life in a place: the plants, animals, fungi and tiny organisms that share a patch of ground and depend on one another. But the word lands differently depending on who you ask.

The scientist's view

To an ecologist, biodiversity is measurable — the number of species, the range of habitats, the genetic richness within a population. More variety usually means a system that copes better when conditions change.

The neighbour's view

To most of us, it is something felt rather than counted: the hum of bees in a verge left to flower, frogs returning to a restored pond, a hedgerow loud with finches. Both views matter, and the corridor needs both.

Why it matters along the B Corridor

The B Corridor exists because nature does not thrive in isolated pockets. Wildlife needs to move, feed and shelter across a connected landscape. When we protect biodiversity along the corridor, a few practical things follow:

  • Pollinators have continuous food from spring to autumn, not just a single flush of flowers.
  • Birds and small mammals can travel safely between green spaces instead of being stranded.
  • Rivers and wetlands stay cleaner, because healthy plant life filters what runs off the land.
  • People gain quieter, greener places to walk, rest and reconnect with the outdoors.
Biodiversity is not something that happens somewhere else, in a far-off rainforest. It is the verge at the end of your road — and it is ours to keep.

Scenes from the corridor

From wet meadows to old churchyards, every stop along the route tells a different part of the story. Swipe through a few of the places where biodiversity is quietly doing its work.

So — what does it mean to you?

Whatever your answer, there is a place for it along the corridor. To explore the species recorded across the country, visit the National Biodiversity Data Centre — or simply come and see the corridor for yourself.

posts.title: 8 July 2026 - Biodiversity Walk & Talk in Riverview Estate
posts.excerpt: B Corridor and Riverview Residents Association host a free biodiversity walk & talk on July 8th at 7pm in Riverview Estate, Dunmore Road, featuring ecologist Ciarán Byrne.
posts.body:
The B Corridor, in partnership with Riverview Residents Association, invites you to a community biodiversity walk and talk event. Join us in Riverview Estate, Dunmore Road, on Wednesday, July 8th at 7pm.

Meeting Point: Green area to the left of the Riverview Estate entrance (opposite Riverside Cottage restaurant and bar).

During the walk, you will learn about the biodiversity-friendly initiatives that Riverview residents have implemented, including a beautiful wooded area that supports local wildlife.

Ecologist Ciarán Byrne, who is developing the Community Biodiversity Action Plan, will share expert advice on enhancing green spaces and gardens in housing estates. Discover practical steps to make your own outdoor areas more wildlife-friendly.

This event is open to all and free of charge. It’s a great opportunity to share your experiences, learn from others, and get inspired for your next biodiversity project.

We hope to see you there.
posts.author: B Corridor Team

posts.title: Wild Bee Festival 2026 comes to Waterford
posts.excerpt: The Wild Bee Festival 2026 takes place in Waterford on 22–23 August, with free talks, walks and workshops celebrating Ireland’s pollinators and how we can help protect them.
posts.body:
Waterford will be buzzing with activity this August as the Wild Bee Festival 2026 arrives at the Waterford Education Support Centre for a free weekend celebrating Ireland’s pollinating insects.

Taking place on Saturday 22nd and Sunday 23rd August 2026, the festival will bring together nature lovers, families, community groups, gardeners, teachers and biodiversity experts to learn more about wild bees and the important role they play in our environment.

The Wild Bee Festival is an annual celebration of pollinating insects and explores practical ways we can all help them survive and thrive in our local communities. Pollinators such as bees, hoverflies, butterflies and moths are essential for healthy ecosystems, food production and wildflower-rich landscapes, but many are under pressure due to habitat loss and environmental change.

Throughout the weekend, visitors can enjoy a varied programme of talks, guided walks and hands-on workshops led by the National Biodiversity Data Centre, B Corridor, and biodiversity specialists. The festival will offer practical advice on how individuals, schools, businesses and local groups can support pollinators by creating more bee-friendly spaces.

Whether you have a garden, a balcony, a community green space or simply an interest in nature, the Wild Bee Festival is a great opportunity to discover how small actions can make a big difference.

The 2026 Wild Bee Festival is coordinated by the National Biodiversity Data Centre in collaboration with B Corridor.

Event details

Date: Saturday 22nd and Sunday 23rd August 2026
Venue: Waterford Education Support Centre, Newtown Road, Waterford, X91 XD98
Admission: Free - you can register here.

For full details of the workshops and talks, see https://pollinators.ie/wild-bee-festival/
posts.author: B Corridor Team

posts.title: B Corridor Summer Social 2026
posts.excerpt: The B Corridor's first Summer Social at Top of the City Garden brought the community together for volunteer talks, poetry by Frank Farrelly, and a celebration of urban biodiversity and collaboration.
posts.body:
For our first-ever Summer Social, the B Corridor community came together at the Top of the City Garden, a biodiversity hub established in 2020. Guests heard from one of the garden’s volunteers about its development, enjoyed poetry readings by local poet Frank Farrelly, and met the resident hens while exploring the space. Light refreshments and lively conversation about the future of the B Corridor rounded out the evening.

The event was a celebration of community collaboration and the value of urban green spaces. Special thanks to the all those involved in preserving this special place.
posts.author: B Corridor Team

posts.title: Wild Bee Festival 2026: The weekend the bees made our case
posts.excerpt: The Wild Bee Festival brought two days of talks and a sunlit walk along the Corridor to Waterford. It also gave our new biodiversity signage its first proper outing.
posts.body:
The Wild Bee Festival came to Waterford on 22 and 23 August. It is run each year by the National Biodiversity Data Centre as part of the All-Ireland Pollinator Plan, and this year it was organised with us here at the B Corridor. Tickets were gone well before the weekend, and people travelled from different parts of Ireland to be there.

Saturday: getting to know our bees

Cecily Maher opened with an introduction to the B Corridor: where our group came from and what we have managed so far. Dr Úna FitzPatrick of the National Biodiversity Data Centre, also co-founder of the All-Ireland Pollinator Plan, followed with an introduction to Ireland’s bees - the groups of species we have here, what each does and how, and how their life cycles work.

Kate Chandler then spoke on how communities can help pollinators. Like every speaker over the weekend, she came back to the same two-part point: what you do on your own patch counts, and it counts for a lot more when your neighbours and community are doing it too. After lunch, Dr Fiona MacGowan drew on her work with Abbeyleix Tidy Towns and a long run of success stories from communities she has worked with - practical, tested, and encouraging if you have ever wondered whether the small steps add up.

Three short talks closed the afternoon. Simon Dowling, who lives along the B Corridor, traced his own route into biodiversity, from caterpillars and a few microhabitats to a garden it eventually took over. 

Brian Jacob told the story of Waterford Trees for Life and their work of “Greening Waterford, one tree at a time”, where the planting matters but educating the next generations is the bigger job. 

Jane Fraher described how the Three Sisters Women’s Shed in Waterford is growing from keeping fabric out of the bin into pollinator-friendly planting, natural dyeing, upcycling, and skills passed between people who might otherwise never have met.

Alongside it all, artist Siobhán Clancy ran the Cross Pollinator Station, a drop-in space for making something by hand, and the Central Library Craft group displayed their biodiversity quilt.

Sunday: out on the Corridor

Sunday began indoors with Micheál Kavanagh of the Déise Men’s Shed and Ciarán Byrne, Senior Ecologist with FERS, on how a community can write its own Biodiversity Action Plan.

Then everyone went outside. Denis Kennedy led a walk along the Corridor and the Maypark nature trail, and the sun came out for it. The pollinator-friendly patches at the start of the route were busy with bees and butterflies, which saved us having to argue the case. It was also the first chance to show the new biodiversity signage to a crowd - you will find the signs at the Glenville, Maypark Village and Ballinakill entrances to the riverwalk.

Thanks

To the National Biodiversity Data Centre, to every speaker who gave up a weekend, to Denis for leading the walk, and to everyone who travelled, asked questions and talked to strangers over the tea and sandwiches. That last part is most of what makes a weekend like this work.

If you are wondering where to start, the All-Ireland Pollinator Plan’s Top Ten Ways to Help Pollinators is a good first stop. If you would like to do something closer to home, get in touch. There is room for everyone along the Corridor.
